name: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester

card.summary: A soothing peptide for sensitive skin with supplier data and one head-to-head trial showing no significant stinging benefit.
card.note: A 2016 capsaicin test found no significant effect for a product containing it.

quick.overview:
Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester is a peptide derivative sold as Calmosensine for sensitive, stinging-prone skin, and appears in some dermatology-brand soothing creams.

Supplier tests report comfort benefits, while a 31-woman capsaicin test of a finished product found no significant effect versus a comparator cream.
quick.mechanism: It is proposed to boost POMC expression, raising alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, which lowers CGRP release and so reduces nerve-driven stinging and inflammation.
quick.risks: No specific adverse events are reported in the review; supplier safety data and CIR assessments are cited. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

lead: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, marketed as Calmosensine (also written Neurosensine), is a synthetic peptide derivative used in soothing skincare for sensitive, reactive skin. Its appearance payoff is calmer, less reactive skin: products containing it aim to reduce the stinging, heat and flushing sensations that go with sensitivity, so that skin looks and feels more comfortable and even.[1]

A 2021 review describes it as derived from the dipeptide Tyr-Arg and proposes that it increases expression of the POMC gene, raising levels of MSH, ACTH and beta-endorphin, which in turn is thought to lower release of CGRP and so reduce stinging indirectly.[1] It appeared in about 5.7 percent of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed, a pool in which peptides overall were found in 17 percent of products.[1][4]

Supplier-reported studies describe reduced heat perception and improved comfort. In the one clinical comparison identified in the review, a 2016 split-face capsaicin test in 31 women, the comparator product containing 4-t-butylcyclohexanol showed lower burning scores at one and two minutes than the product containing acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, and the review notes the product bases differed.[1][2]
infobox: La Roche-Posay Toleriane Ultra Intense Soothing Care [2]

paras: The review reports no direct TRPV1 action; the proposed route runs through melanocortin receptors (via alpha-MSH) and the opioid pathway (via beta-endorphin) [1]. In vitro reports cited there include raised aquaporin-3, filaggrin, caspase 14 and keratin 10 expression and reduced PGE2 and NF-kB signalling [1].

The ingredient is used in facial products marketed for sensitive skin, an issue more than 50 percent of adults report according to the introduction of one dermatology paper.[3] The 2021 review found the available efficacy data for such peptides mostly in patents and supplier brochures rather than randomized placebo-controlled studies, with only one clinical study in volunteers with sensitive skin.[4] A 2022 survey of 88 sensitive-skin products from 19 multinational brands ranked niacinamide, panthenol and other actives most common and described clinical studies on these ingredients as sparse.[5]
Supplier-reported studies cited in the review include a 3 percent cream reducing heat perception in 21 volunteers and a double-blind sandpaper test in 18 volunteers reporting greater comfort [1].

A single-blind, randomized split-face capsaicin-stinging test in 31 women aged 19 to 65 with self-perceived sensitive skin compared Eucerin UltraSensitive Soothing Care (4-t-butylcyclohexanol) with La Roche-Posay Toleriane Ultra Intense Soothing Care (acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester), applying each to a nasolabial fold.[2] All subjects reported stinging after capsaicin; the 4-t-butylcyclohexanol product gave significantly lower burning at one and two minutes after application than the acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester product.[2] The review notes the creams differed in other respects.[1] A companion 2016 paper found in vitro that 4-t-butylcyclohexanol reduced TRPV1 activation while acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester had no effect on the receptor.[3]
The review reports no specific adverse events and cites supplier safety data sheets and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review for topical safety [1].

angle.text: Used in leave-on creams for sensitive skin, it is marketed to calm discomfort and reactivity so skin looks more settled. The proposed mechanism is indirect, via opioid and melanocortin signalling.
